intro.metaDescription: A Practice of Hope. The Compassionate Curriculum is a participatory framework for learning, reflection, and collective growth.
intro.heading: Introduction: A Practice of Hope
intro.p1: The Compassionate Curriculum is a participatory framework for learning, reflection, and collective growth, designed with and for people with lived experience of trauma or any form of structural harm. It draws on the idea that lived experience is a form of knowledge, and that healing, critical understanding, and imagination are all necessary for building more just futures.
intro.p2: Rather than asking participants simply to receive information, the curriculum invites them to shape meaning together. It is grounded in shared authorship, mutual aid, and an ethic of accountability. It is also strengths-based. The work does not begin from what people lack, but from what they already know, have survived, and can build together. Across the curriculum, participants are encouraged to reflect on their own experience, listen to one another, and practice forms of collective learning that can support both personal transformation and broader social change.
intro.p3Intro: The curriculum has three connected sections.
intro.p3MidBeloved: focuses on identity, belonging, emotional fluency, and historical trauma. It helps participants better understand themselves, their relationships, and the wider systems that shape how they move through the world.
intro.p3MidRestorative: introduces circles, active listening, reauthoring, and other tools that support trust, reflection, accountability, and shared responsibility.
intro.p3MidMedia: explores storytelling, representation, and imagination. It invites participants to examine dominant narratives, tell fuller stories about themselves, and build imaginative capacity for creative problem solving and future making.
intro.p4: The Compassionate Curriculum is designed as an open and living framework. It can be used in universities, community organizations, advocacy spaces, research settings, and other group contexts where facilitators want to support belonging, dialogue, and collaborative learning. Some groups may use it as a structured series of workshops. Others may draw on individual sections or activities and adapt them to local needs.
intro.p5: At its core, the curriculum is guided by participation, embodiment, storytelling, and multimodal learning. It aims to create conditions in which people can think critically, connect across differences, and imagine otherwise together. In this sense, the Compassionate Curriculum is not only a set of exercises, but a way of practicing mutual support, shared inquiry, and hope in common.

about.heading: About
about.p1: The Compassionate Curriculum is a participatory framework for learning, reflection, and collective growth, designed with and for people with lived experience of trauma or any form of structural harm. It draws on the idea that lived experience is a form of knowledge, and that healing, critical understanding, and imagination are all necessary for building more just futures.
about.p2: Rather than asking participants simply to receive information, the curriculum invites them to shape meaning together. It is grounded in shared authorship, mutual aid, and an ethic of accountability.
about.story1: The Compassionate Curriculum began in an unlikely place: a small kitchen at Altcourse Prison in Liverpool, where incarcerated veterans, arts workers, a social scientist, and justice sector policymakers sat together in a circle of plastic chairs and started imagining what "coming home" could really mean. That first gathering was part of Melanie Crean's A Machine to Unmake You (2019–2024), an art and pedagogical project commissioned by FACT Liverpool, through which participants used storytelling, silent performance, and collaborative futuring to design their own systems of care rather than have systems designed for them.
about.story2: Out of those workshops came a shared vision for a university "pod" system: small, cohort-based groups where students affected by carceral systems could move through a creative, strengths-based curriculum together, one built not only to support their own path through education, but to prepare them to mentor and support others coming up behind them. That vision became the Compassionate Curriculum. It opens by naming the structural harms such as racism, gender-based discrimination, economic inequality, and ableism that so often shape people's experience of trauma. From there it builds strengths-based practice: circle work, reauthoring, active listening, trauma informed facilitation. And it closes by turning toward the future, examining bias in how people are represented, then building the imaginative and creative problem-solving skills participants need to picture, and start building, something better.
about.story3: The curriculum is designed to be lived, not just read, and a framework that grows through use. In keeping with the "credible messenger" model at its heart, the people who first encounter it as learners are meant to become the people who carry it forward.
about.story4: When we imagine alongside people in prison, that imagining comes with a responsibility that does not end when the workshop does. The hopes and ideas shared in that first kitchen at Altcourse were not ours to simply gather and move on from. We hold ourselves accountable to carrying them forward, doing what we can, from wherever we sit, to help realise what was imagined together. Anything less would turn that act of imagining into something extractive: taking people's hopes without any obligation to act on them.
about.ack1: The Compassionate Curriculum is led by Melanie Crean and Emma Murray, alongside a dedicated working group consisting of Dominique Walker, Dianne Garrison, Sian Phillips, and Paula Harriott.
